Designated Use & Purpose

Repurposing a food utensil for non-food use: It is debated whether a food utensil bought for food but subsequently reappropriated for a non-food purpose requires tevilah (e.g., a food knife used for cutting paper). A Rav should be consulted.
Temporary non-food use before tevila: If one wants to use cups to hold Chanukah oil before immersing the cups, most poskim rule this is permitted since it is not a food-use. Pri Eliyahu (vol. 3, no. 25) rules that this should not be done.
Occasional food use — tevila without a brocha: Utensils that are only occasionally used for food and mostly for other purposes should be immersed without a blessing.
Non-food utensil used occasionally for food: A utensil that was not manufactured for food from the very outset may be occasionally used for food without tevilah.
Initial food preparation tools — tevila without a brocha: Utensils used in the initial stages of food preparation — kneading utensils, grinders, shechita knives — should be immersed without a blessing.
Cooking pot requires tevila even if food is removed early: A cooking pot requires immersion with a blessing even if the owner's intention is to remove the food from the pot before it becomes edible.

Mixed Materials & Coatings

Indirect contact exempts from tevila: If there is a separation between the food and utensil, the utensil is exempt from immersion — for example, tripods or grates that support cooking utensils. Simply wrapping a cloth or piece of paper around food does not exempt the container in which it is placed.
Two-material utensil: follow the food-contact material: A utensil manufactured from two materials — one requiring immersion (e.g., metal) and one exempt (e.g., wood) — requires immersion only if the non-exempt material comes into direct contact with food, and the utensil is not functional without the non-exempt material.
Exempt material held together with interior nails: An exempt material (e.g., wood) held together with nails on the inside requires immersion if it cannot function without the nails.
Metal coating on both sides — tevila with a brocha: An exempt material coated with metal on the inside and outside requires immersion and a blessing. If coated only for decorative purposes, or only on the inside with metal, immersion should be done without a blessing. If coated only on the outside, immersion is not required.
Large earthenware with interior metal coating: Some authorities exempt large earthenware utensils coated with metal only on the inside from immersion, due to their great size. One who is stringent should not recite a blessing.
Glass coating on both sides — tevila without a brocha: An exempt material coated with glass on the inside and outside should be immersed without a blessing.
Exempt coating on a metal utensil: A utensil requiring immersion that is coated with an exempt material for functional purposes should be immersed without a blessing. If coated only for decorative purposes, immersion should be done with a blessing.
Paint does not change tevila status: Coloring a utensil with paint does not change its status regarding tevilah, as the paint is considered part of the utensil.

Disposables, Size & Special Forms

Disposable utensils do not require tevila: Utensils that are thrown away after use — disposable plates, cups, and the like, and utensils manufactured from aluminum foil — do not require immersion. The temporary use of utensils without immersion is only forbidden if the utensil could be used on a regular basis; utensils unfit for long-term use are not considered functional keilim.
Storage bottles and containers: Bottles or containers used for storing food or drink require immersion with a blessing, provided the food stored in them is unwrapped. If these containers are not normally brought to the table, a blessing is not recited.
Shape of the utensil is irrelevant: The shape of utensils (e.g., a spoon versus a knife) does not play a role in their status regarding the halachos of tevilah.
Utensil secured to the ground — debated: It is debated whether a utensil secured to the ground, floor, or wall is exempt from immersion. Some authorities do not require immersion for utensils designed to function more effectively when fastened to the ground. A Rav should be consulted.
Vessel over 40 se'ah — possible exemption: Some poskim exempt metal utensils with a capacity of more than 40 se'ah (331–921 liters / 87.5–243 gallons). One who is stringent should not recite a blessing.

Factory & Manufacturer Ownership

Non-Jewish factory: tevila with a brocha required: A utensil manufactured in a factory owned by non-Jews requires immersion with a blessing, whether ownership is vested in a public corporation, private corporation, or a government. It makes no difference whether the workers are Jewish or non-Jewish.
Jewish-owned factory: no tevila required: A utensil purchased from a factory owned by a Jew does not require immersion even if the workforce is non-Jewish hourly workers. If the employees are non-Jewish artisan workers paid by piece (per unit), immersion without a blessing is required, since an artisan gains a share in his product as he works.
Joint Jewish/non-Jewish factory: tevila with a brocha: A utensil manufactured in a factory jointly owned by a Jew and a non-Jew requires immersion with a blessing. The same applies to factories owned by a corporation with both Jewish and non-Jewish shareholders.
Purchased from a Jewish retailer: verify the manufacturer: When a utensil is purchased from a Jewish retailer, one should ascertain whether the manufacturer is Jewish. If this cannot be determined, immersion is required whether the majority of factories in that country are owned by Jews or non-Jews. The blessing is recited only if the majority of factories are at least partially non-Jewish. Utensils imported from Israel where most manufacturers are Jewish, and not purchased through non-Jewish middlemen, generally do not require immersion.

Artisan Work, Repairs & Modifications

Non-Jewish artisan commissioned with Jewish-supplied metal: A utensil commissioned from a non-Jewish artisan and made from metal supplied by a Jew requires immersion without a blessing. If part of the metal was supplied by a non-Jew, most authorities require immersion with a blessing. If most of the metal was supplied by a non-Jew, all authorities require immersion with a blessing.
Broken utensil repaired by a non-Jew: A utensil that is broken or perforated and no longer usable loses its status as a utensil. If repaired by a non-Jew with his own metal, immersion with a blessing is required. If the metal is supplied by a Jew, immersion without a blessing is required.
Perforated vessel repaired after alternate use: A perforated drinking utensil being used for another purpose (e.g., to hold fruit) does not require immersion when repaired by a non-Jew, even if it is subsequently used again for liquids (Pri Megadim, cited by Darchei Teshuva 120:78).
Filling originally-designed holes does not obligate tevila: A utensil whose original design included holes does not require immersion if the holes are filled in by a non-Jew. Since the utensil was not broken, filling the holes is not considered manufacturing.
Non-Jew coats or re-plates the utensil: A utensil coated by a non-Jew with a material requiring immersion — for instance, re-silvering — should be immersed without a blessing.
Non-Jew repairs handles — tevila without a brocha: If the handles of cutlery are repaired by a non-Jew, it would seem that it should be immersed without a blessing. A Rav should be consulted.
Knife sharpened by a non-Jew: no re-immersion needed: A knife sharpened by a non-Jew does not require immersion.

Gifts, Transfers & Purchasing

Jewish artisan makes for non-Jew; Jew purchases: A utensil manufactured by a Jewish artisan for a non-Jew with metal supplied by the non-Jew requires immersion with a blessing if the artisan purchases the utensil from the non-Jew after finishing it. Some authorities argue a blessing is not recited. If the Jew supplied part of the metal, opinions vary.
Made by one Jew for another using non-Jewish metal: A utensil manufactured by one Jew for another Jew with metal purchased from a non-Jew does not require immersion. A utensil purchased from a non-Jew and melted down and refashioned by a Jew does not require immersion.
Gift from a non-Jew: tevila with a brocha required: A utensil received as a gift from a non-Jew requires immersion and a blessing.
Gift or purchase from a Jew (non-Jewish manufacture): A utensil purchased or received as a gift from a Jew that was manufactured by a non-Jew requires immersion with a blessing (assuming it was not yet immersed).
Trial purchase — not yet obligated: A utensil purchased on trial does not require immersion until the purchase is finalized.
Credit purchase — disputed: The immersion requirement of utensils purchased on credit is questionable, since a rabbinic method of acquisition may not affect a biblical requirement of immersion. That said, if a glass utensil (whose obligation is rabbinic) is bought on credit, or if a metal utensil is bought on credit and brought home first (kinyan chatzer), all would agree immersion is required with a blessing. This is not to be confused with modern credit card transactions, where the seller is paid immediately.
Sold to a non-Jew and repurchased: tevila required: A Jewish utensil sold or gifted to a non-Jew and subsequently repurchased by a Jew requires immersion with a blessing. If the non-Jew bought the item but never actually took possession of it, this is debated — a Rav should be consulted. For this reason, chametz utensils should not be sold to a non-Jew for Pesach; instead, only the chametz particles should be sold, or the utensil merely rented or lent.
Loaned to a non-Jew and returned: tevila without a brocha: A utensil given by a Jew to a non-Jew on condition that it be returned requires immersion without a blessing when returned. Similarly, a utensil given by a non-Jew to a Jew on condition it be returned should be immersed without a blessing before use.
Joint ownership with a non-Jew exempts from tevila: A utensil owned jointly by a Jew and a non-Jew does not require immersion. One should not purposely do this to dodge the mitzvah. Furthermore, the non-Jewish partner would need a substantial share and actually makes use of the utensils. If the Jew purchases the non-Jew's share, immersion with a blessing is required.
Israeli public authority utensils: tevila with a brocha: Utensils purchased or captured from non-Jews and owned by a public authority in the State of Israel (Army, Government, or Local Authority) require immersion with a blessing. Even though there are non-Jewish citizens of the state, the utensils are considered to have come into Jewish possession.
Non-Jew renounces ownerless utensil: Jew must tovel: If a non-Jew renounces ownership of a utensil (hefker) and a Jew takes possession of it with intention to acquire it, immersion is required. If the Jew does not intend to acquire it, the utensil may be used without immersion.
Not acquiring an ownerless utensil: may use without tevila: One can intend not to acquire an ownerless (hefker) utensil and use it without immersion. However, one cannot simply make his own utensil ownerless and then use it while intending not to reacquire it.

Borrowing, Renting & Commercial Use

Borrowed or rented from a non-Jew: no tevila: A Jew who borrows or rents a utensil from a non-Jew may use it without immersion. A utensil belonging to a Jew borrowed or rented by a non-Jew does not require immersion when returned, since the Jew is still considered the owner.
Borrowed from a Jew: tevila required before use: A Jew who borrows or rents utensils requiring immersion from another Jew may not use them without immersion. For this reason, eating or drinking directly from utensils that require immersion in someone else's home should be avoided. Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach offers a rationale to permit a guest to eat from a host's plates, but cautions against forks, spoons, or drinking cups.
Commercial rental utensils: borrower may use without tevila: Commercial utensils purchased by a Jew for lending or renting may be used by the borrower or renter without immersion — they are considered commercial utensils that do not require immersion. Since there is doubt regarding this halacha, one who is stringent should not recite a brocha.
Purchased for food but then lent: obligation already applies: A utensil purchased for food but lent or rented instead requires immersion. The obligation took effect at the time of purchase. The same ruling applies if it is subsequently sold to another person who intends to lend it out.
Borrowed from a minor: no tevila required: A utensil borrowed or rented from a minor does not require immersion.
From an apostate or Shabbos-violating Jew: Utensils manufactured by Jews and purchased from an apostate Jew or from a Jew who publicly transgresses Shabbos do not require immersion. Some authorities are stringent. One who wishes to act stringently should not recite a blessing.
Pre-conversion utensils: tevila without a brocha: Utensils owned by a non-Jew before he converted to Judaism require immersion without a blessing.

Using Utensils Before Tevila

Unimmersed utensils may be kept but not used: Utensils may be kept in the house before immersion, but they may not be used for eating or cooking even on a temporary basis.
Training children (chinuch) not to use unimmersed utensils: A parent should train their child (chinuch) to refrain from using utensils before immersion. It is forbidden for anyone — parent or stranger — to serve a child or instruct him to eat from an unimmersed utensil. A stranger is not obligated to stop a child from using an unimmersed utensil on his own. When necessary, food for which one has a special need may be served to a minor from a utensil that cannot be immersed.
Non-food utensil may be used for food without tevila: A utensil not manufactured to be used for food may be used occasionally for eating without immersion.
Utensil used exclusively by non-Jews: no tevila required: A utensil purchased by a Jew but used only by non-Jews does not require immersion.
Food cooked in an unimmersed utensil remains kosher: If one cooked in a utensil before immersing it, the food may still be eaten. The food should be removed from the utensil as soon as possible. There is discussion on food cans and jars: some rule that once opened, contents should be removed immediately; others permit even eating directly from the container, since most people do not intend to acquire the actual container.
May not instruct others to use an unimmersed utensil: One may not instruct a non-Jew (or another Jew) to prepare food for him with a utensil lacking immersion.
Utensil that cannot be immersed: break and have a Jew repair it: A utensil purchased from a non-Jew that cannot be immersed should be broken (so it loses the status of a utensil) and then repaired by a Jew. For example, a very large cauldron should be perforated and then repaired by a Jew.
Electrical appliance workaround: dismantle and reassemble: An electrical appliance that cannot be immersed should be dismantled so that it can no longer be used without repair by an electrician. Once reassembled, it will be 'manufactured' by a Jew and exempt from immersion. Some say this method should only be used for electrical appliances. Consult a Rav about the required degree of dismantling.
Multi-part utensil does not lose its status when dismantled: A utensil composed of different parts, like a meat grinder, does not lose the status of a utensil when it is dismantled.

Doubt, Mixtures & Chatzitzah (Barriers)

When in doubt: immerse without a brocha: Whenever there is a doubt as to whether a utensil has undergone immersion or whether it requires immersion, the utensil should be immersed without a blessing.
Immersed and unimmersed utensils mixed: all must be immersed: If one or more utensils requiring immersion become mixed up with utensils that do not require immersion and one cannot tell the difference, all of them should be immersed. The plural blessing ('al tevilas keilim') is recited even if only one utensil requires immersion. If immersing all would be a great bother or expense, and most utensils do not require immersion, one can rely on bitul b'rov.
A barrier (chatzitzah) invalidates the immersion: A chatzitzah — an interposition between the utensil and the water — invalidates the immersion.
Prepare the utensil: remove dirt, rust, labels, and residue: Dirt, rust, seals, and black spots caused by fire must be removed. Labels that are not usually removed — for instance, labels on crystal that enhance its value — are considered part of the utensil and need not be removed. Limestone accumulated inside a kettle is not a chatzitzah, since people are not particular about removing it.
Re-immersion after discovering a chatzitzah: A utensil immersed with a chatzitzah must be immersed a second time after the chatzitzah is removed, without a blessing. If the owner became distracted between the first and second immersion, a new blessing should be recited.
Minor or non-bothersome chatzitzah does not invalidate: A chatzitzah attached to a minority of a utensil, or one that neither the owner nor most other people are particular about removing, does not render the immersion ineffective. Therefore, storekeepers who leave price labels on during immersion — since they prefer the label to stay for customers — need not perform another immersion. One should initially remove such chatzitzos.
Intermittent concern about a chatzitzah: must still remove it: A chatzitzah that is sometimes considered bothersome and sometimes not must still be removed before immersion, even if the person is not currently bothered by it.
Handles and attached parts are not a chatzitzah: Handles and other parts attached to a utensil — even those made from exempt materials — do not have to be removed before immersion. Any chatzitzos on them must be removed. Therefore, a bottle encased in a wicker basket may be immersed since the basket is not considered a chatzitzah. Similarly, there is no need to take apart a thermos or other assembled utensils.
Incorrectly attached part is considered a chatzitzah: A part that is attached to a utensil incorrectly is considered a chatzitzah, because it will eventually be removed and reattached properly.
Kasher the utensil before immersing it: A utensil that needs to be kashered should be kashered before tevilah. Some say that if the order was switched, the tevilah should be repeated after kashering without a blessing.

Shabbos, Yom Tov & Timing

Tevila may not be performed on Shabbos or Yom Tov: Utensils may be immersed any day or night except Shabbos and Yom Tov. Tevilah enables a utensil to be used, which constitutes 'repairing' the utensil and is therefore forbidden on Shabbos and Yom Tov (there are certain exceptions).
Tevila on Chol HaMoed is permitted: Tevilah is permitted during Chol HaMoed.
Forgot to tovel before Shabbos: give to a non-Jew and borrow back: If a person forgets to immerse a utensil before Shabbos or Yom Tov, he may give it to a non-Jew as a gift (the non-Jew should acquire it through meshichah or hagbahah) and borrow it back. After Shabbos or when a mikvah is available, the utensils should be immersed. This method should only be used in pressing circumstances. It is advisable to ask the non-Jew to return the utensil as a gift so it may then be immersed with a blessing.
Tevila on Yom Tov permitted discreetly if unavoidable: If tevilah could not be performed before Yom Tov and the utensil is necessary for the enjoyment of the holiday, tevilah may be carried out with a blessing on Yom Tov itself (but not Shabbos) in the normal manner. It must be done discreetly and not publicized.
Transgressed and immersed on Shabbos: tevila is valid: Someone who transgresses by immersing a utensil on Shabbos or Yom Tov as if they were normal days may use it.
Tevila during twilight (bein hashmashos) is generally prohibited: Tevilah is prohibited during the twilight before Shabbos or Yom Tov (Bein Hashmashos). Someone in doubt as to whether it is twilight should not immerse a utensil. A utensil needed for Shabbos or Yom Tov may be immersed with a blessing during the twilight before Shabbos or Yom Tov. Tevilah during the twilight that precedes Motzo'ei Shabbos or Motzo'ei Yom Tov is forbidden.
Accepted Shabbos early: may not immerse: A person who accepts Shabbos or Yom Tov before sunset may not immerse utensils. He may, however, ask another Jew who has not yet accepted Shabbos, or a non-Jew supervised by a Jew, to immerse them.
After Shabbos — using utensils before Havdala: A person who has not yet made Havdala on Motzo'ei Shabbos may ask a Jew who has to immerse his utensils for him. He may then use them before reciting Havdala.

Valid Waters & Who May Perform Tevila

Requires a mikvah valid for niddah: Tevilas Keilim must be performed in water suitable for the tevilah of a woman who is a niddah — the sea, ocean, a mikvah, a river, or a large collection of rain water containing 40 se'ah. Immersion cannot be done in drawn water or even in a large utensil that filled with the necessary amount of water on its own.
Immersion in snow: only in pressing circumstances: Utensils may not be immersed in snow. In pressing circumstances, glassware and coated earthenware may be immersed in snow if 40 se'ah are collected in one place and each utensil is completely covered without any airspace separating it from the snow.
Any person may tovel — but a Jewish adult must supervise: Anyone — Jews, non-Jews, minors — may immerse a utensil. An adult Jew must supervise a minor or a non-Jew performing tevilah, as their testimony regarding tevilas keilim is not accepted. Even a utensil that falls into a kosher mikvah by accident undergoes a valid tevilah. It is proper to have intention to fulfill the mitzvah during its performance.
Non-Jew may not recite the brocha when immersing: Utensils requiring immersion with a blessing should not be given to a non-Jew to immerse even with Jewish adult supervision, since the Jew cannot recite a blessing over tevilah performed by a non-Jew. If the Jew is immersing other utensils simultaneously, he may recite the blessing over his own utensils with intention to include those being immersed by the non-Jew.
Tevila done without the owner's knowledge is valid: Tevilah performed without the owner's knowledge is effective. A person who knows the owner will be pleased to learn his utensils were immersed may recite the blessing even if not formally designated as an agent.
Storekeeper should not tovel merchandise before sale: A Jewish storekeeper who sells utensils manufactured by non-Jews should not immerse them before they are purchased. Commercial utensils become subject to tevilah only after they are sold.
Do not tovel a gift utensil before presenting it: A utensil purchased for a gift should not be immersed before it is given to the recipient.

The Brocha — Recitation & Rules

Tovel plastic stringently: no brocha recited: Those who act stringently and immerse nylon and plastic utensils should not recite a blessing.
Plural/singular blessing mismatch is valid post-facto: One who recites the plural form of the blessing when immersing one utensil, or the singular form when immersing multiple utensils, has fulfilled the obligation.
If uncertain whether brocha was recited: do not repeat it: One who is uncertain whether he has recited the blessing should not recite it.
Brocha must be recited before immersion, not after: One who did not recite the blessing before immersion should not recite it after.
A minor performing tevila recites the brocha: A minor who performs tevilah recites a blessing.
Additional utensil found mid-session: recite a separate brocha: A person in the process of immersing utensils who finds after reciting the blessing that he needs to immerse another utensil should recite a separate blessing for the additional utensil after finishing with the first.
Seller must inform buyer of immersion status: A Jew who sells used utensils that have already been immersed, or utensils manufactured in a Jewish factory that are thus exempt, must inform purchasers so they will not recite unnecessary blessings. Conversely, it is advisable for vendors of utensils that require tevilah to inform purchasers of this fact.
When in doubt whether tevila is required: no brocha: When there is a doubt as to whether or not a utensil should be immersed, a blessing is not recited.
Doubtful utensil: immerse together with a definite one: Utensils that do not require a blessing when immersed (e.g., those over whose immersion the recitation of the blessing is debated) should be immersed together with utensils that do require a blessing. The blessing should be recited in the plural form and the utensil that definitely requires tevilah should be immersed first.
Accidentally recited a brocha for a doubtful utensil: proceed: A person who accidentally recited a blessing before immersing a utensil when the obligation of tevilah was questionable should still not make any interruption between the blessing and tevilah.
Utensils requiring tevila without a brocha: Among those utensils which require tevilah without a blessing: utensils in which food is not normally brought to an edible stage (kneading implements, meat grinders, shechita knives), and food containers that are not used for preparing food or for eating/drinking and are not brought to the table.
Hold the utensil in the dominant hand during the brocha: The utensil should be held in the right hand during the recitation of the blessing. A left-handed person should hold it in their left hand. Although the blessing may be recited while sitting, some authorities recommend standing.
Concentrate fully during the brocha: A person should concentrate totally on the words being recited and certainly not be involved in any other activity.
A naked person may not recite a brocha: A naked person may not recite a blessing, even with closed eyes. A blessing may not be recited in the presence of a naked person unless the person reciting it turns away his body and face.
Recite the brocha outside if there is a foul odor inside: If reciting the blessing in the mikvah room is not possible due to some foul odor, the blessing should be recited just outside and then the utensil immediately brought inside and immersed.
Two people immersing: one recites for both: When two people are immersing utensils, it is recommended that one of them recites the blessing. The listener must hear the entire blessing and intend to fulfill his obligation through listening; he should respond 'Amen.' He should not respond 'baruch hu u'varuch shemo' during the blessing. If the reciter's utensil breaks between the blessing and the immersion, or if he speaks in between, the blessing is still valid on behalf of the other person.
One person immersing: another may not recite on their behalf: If only one person is immersing utensils, another person should not recite the blessing on his behalf unless the former is a minor who does not know how to recite a blessing.
Designated agent recites the brocha on behalf of the owner: When a person designates an agent to immerse utensils for him, the agent recites the blessing.
Singular-form brocha heard by another covers multiple utensils: A person immersing two utensils — where the blessing is 'al tevilas keilim' (plural) — can fulfill the obligation by listening to someone recite 'al tevilas keili' (singular, for one utensil).

Physical Technique of Immersion

Do not speak between the brocha and the immersion: One should be careful not to speak even one word between the blessing and tevilah. If one speaks about matters not pertaining to the tevilah, a new blessing is required.
Avoid pausing between the brocha and the immersion: It is advisable that there be no pause, even a silent one, between the blessing and tevilah. As long as the person does not become distracted, the blessing is not repeated.
No interruption required between successive immersions: When more than one utensil is being immersed, there should be no interruption between immersions. If one speaks about matters not pertaining to the tevilah, a new blessing is not required.
Water must reach the entire utensil simultaneously: Water must reach all parts of the utensil, inside and out. Tevilah is not effective when one part of the utensil is immersed and only then the other part — even if the utensil is so large that it cannot be immersed at one time. It must be totally submerged all at once.
Hold utensils loosely so water reaches all surfaces: The utensils should be held loosely during tevilah so that the immerser's hand does not create a chatzitzah. If one wishes to grasp the utensil tightly, he should either change his grasp while it is underwater (so water reaches all parts in the process), or place his hand in the water first and then rest the utensil on it.
Utensils may be immersed inside a basket or another utensil: Utensils may be placed inside a netted sack, basket, or another utensil and then immersed. A number of utensils may be placed next to one another (not on top of one another). Tevilah of a utensil inside another is effective only when the opening of the outer utensil is at least two finger-breadths wide (approx. 5 cm / 2 inches).
Utensils tied together may be immersed together: Utensils may be immersed when they are loosely tied together with string or rope. A loose knot should be used even if it is only tied to the handles.
Handles are considered part of the utensil: A handle attached to a utensil is considered part of that utensil and requires tevilah, even if made from a material that doesn't require tevilah. Attaching a handle to a utensil that has already been immersed does not necessitate a second tevilah.
Immerse the entire utensil even if part is made of exempt material: When part of the utensil requiring tevilah is made from material that does not require tevilah, the whole utensil should be immersed.
Utensils with detachable parts should be immersed fully assembled: It is best to immerse utensils with detachable parts — such as a meat grinder or thermos — when fully assembled in functional form. If parts are immersed separately, they should be completely taken apart (including every screw). Utensils with substitute parts (e.g., different blades) should be immersed with one part attached, then again with another, until all blades have been immersed.
Pocket knife must be immersed open: A pocket knife should be immersed open. If there are multiple blades, it should be immersed with one blade open, then again with another, until all blades have been immersed.
Immerse receptacles sideways or face-up, not face-down: Utensils that are receptacles (like glasses) may be immersed sideways or face-up. If immersed face-down, the air pocket may prevent water from reaching inside, rendering the tevilah invalid. Utensils with wide openings (like plates or wide, shallow pots) can be immersed face-up or down.
Fill narrow-necked bottles before immersing: Utensils with narrow openings (like bottles) should either be filled with tap water before immersion, or left in the mikvah long enough to fill with water. Some say it is better practice to fill the bottle beforehand than to rely on the cessation of rising air bubbles as proof the bottle is filled.
Minimum water coverage: enough to moisten other objects: The minimum amount of water that must cover the utensil during tevilah is enough to enable the utensil to moisten other objects.
One complete immersion is sufficient: It is sufficient to immerse a utensil once.
Have intention to fulfill the mitzvah: When immersing the utensil it is proper to have intention to fulfill the mitzvah of tevilas keilim and to remove the non-Jewish impurity from the utensil. The immersion is valid even if performed without any intention whatsoever.
